title: Bounded-below objects detect isomorphisms in sheaf derived categories
statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be a small site, let $\mathcal O$ be a sheaf of commutative rings, and let $\mathcal A=\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal O)$ [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. Work in its ordinary unbounded derived category $D(\mathcal A)$ [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Say $H$ is bounded below if $H^q(H)=0$ for all sufficiently negative $q$. If a morphism $\alpha:B\to G$ induces bijections $\operatorname{Hom}(H[n],B)\to\operatorname{Hom}(H[n],G)$ for every bounded-below object $H$ and every $n\in\mathbf Z$, then $\alpha$ is an isomorphism. No boundedness hypothesis is imposed on $B$ or $G$.

source.place: Final composition/open-locality paragraph: bounded-below representing-object test

proof.text: Fix any object $X\in D(\mathcal A)$ and represent it by a complex $K^\bullet$, so $X\cong QK^\bullet$. For $r\in\mathbf N$ put $E_r^\bullet=\sigma_{\ge-r}K^\bullet$: its term in degree $i$ is zero for $i<-r$ and $K^i$ otherwise, with the retained differentials. These are subcomplexes, with inclusions $E_r^\bullet\to E_{r+1}^\bullet$. Each $QE_r^\bullet$ has zero cohomology in degrees below $-r$, hence is an allowed bounded-below test object. In each fixed degree $i$ the sequence is eventually the constant diagram $K^i$ with identity transitions. Its colimit is $K^i$: a cocone factors uniquely by its stable value. These factorizations commute with the differentials because the original cocone maps do. Thus the degreewise colimit of the $E_r^\bullet$ is $K^\bullet$.

source.place: Tag 0118 (homology-section-truncations), cochain stupid lower truncation; degreewise eventual-constant cocone argument

proof.text: Apply [lem-kun-complex-colimit-hocolim] to this sequence in $\mathcal A=\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal O)$. It applies to a sheaf of commutative rings on any small site and has no boundedness hypothesis. It identifies $P=Q(\bigoplus_{r\ge0}E_r^\bullet)$ with the coproduct $\bigoplus_{r\ge0}QE_r^\bullet$ in the ordinary unbounded derived category. Its last assertion, transported along $QK^\bullet\cong X$, supplies a distinguished triangle $P\xrightarrow{u}P\xrightarrow{j}X\xrightarrow{d}P[1]$, where $u=1-s$ and $s$ is induced by the consecutive inclusions. This provides an actual coproduct and triangle, rather than an assertion that ordinary colimits in the derived category compute $X$.

source.place: Tags 0949 (derived-lemma-colim-hocolim), 090Z (derived-definition-derived-colimit); module-sheaf telescope statement of the cited node

proof.text: The composites of consecutive arrows of this triangle and its rotations vanish. Here is the elementary TR3 argument: for any distinguished $A\xrightarrow{a}B\xrightarrow{b}C\to A[1]$, map the distinguished identity triangle $A\xrightarrow{1}A\to0\to A[1]$ into it using $1_A,a$ on the first two vertices. TR3 supplies the third map, necessarily zero, so its second square gives $ba=0$. Rotate to get the other zero composites. In particular $ju=0$, $dj=0$, and $vd=0$ for $v=-u[1]:P[1]\to P[1]$, the third arrow of the rotated triangle $P\xrightarrow{j}X\xrightarrow{d}P[1]\xrightarrow{v}P[1]$.

source.place: Tag 0146 (derived-lemma-composition-zero), proof using TR3 and rotation

proof.text: For $W=B,G$, the coproduct universal property identifies $\operatorname{Hom}(P,W)$ with $\prod_r\operatorname{Hom}(QE_r^\bullet,W)$. Under these identifications postcomposition by $\alpha$ is the product of the assumed bijections (use shift $n=0$), and so is bijective: invert each coordinate. The shift is an automorphism, hence $\operatorname{Hom}(P[1],W)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(P,W[-1])\cong\prod_r\operatorname{Hom}(QE_r^\bullet[1],W)$. Thus postcomposition by $\alpha$ is also bijective on $\operatorname{Hom}(P[1],-)\,$, using the hypothesis at shift $n=1$. Only the universal property of a coproduct is used; there is no compactness or commutation of Hom with a filtered colimit assumption.

source.place: Tag 090Z (derived-definition-derived-colimit); coproduct universal property and shift equivalence

proof.text: To prove surjectivity on $\operatorname{Hom}(X,-)$, take $g:X\to G$. By step 4 lift $gj:P\to G$ to $b:P\to B$. Then $\alpha bu=gju=0$, so injectivity on $\operatorname{Hom}(P,-)$ gives $bu=0$. Clause (i) of [lem-weil-pbc-hom-out-of-triangle-exact] for $P\xrightarrow{u}P\xrightarrow{j}X$ gives $c:X\to B$ with $cj=b$. The residual $g-\alpha c$ vanishes after precomposition with $j$. Clause (ii) gives $k:P[1]\to G$ with $g-\alpha c=kd$. Lift $k$ to $l:P[1]\to B$ by step 4. Now $\alpha(c+ld)=g$, which proves surjectivity.

source.place: Tag 0149 (derived-lemma-representable-homological), clauses (i) and (ii) of cited node; explicit surjectivity chase

proof.text: For injectivity take $f:X\to B$ with $\alpha f=0$. Injectivity on $\operatorname{Hom}(P,-)$ gives $fj=0$. Clause (ii) of [lem-weil-pbc-hom-out-of-triangle-exact] gives $k:P[1]\to B$ with $f=kd$. Since $(\alpha k)d=0$, clause (ii) applied to the rotated triangle $P\xrightarrow{j}X\xrightarrow{d}P[1]\xrightarrow{v}P[1]$ gives $r:P[1]\to G$ with $\alpha k=rv$. Lift $r$ to $t:P[1]\to B$ by step 4. Then $\alpha(k-tv)=0$, so injectivity on $\operatorname{Hom}(P[1],-)$ gives $k=tv$. Consequently $f=tvd=0$ by step 3. Taking the difference of two maps proves injectivity. Together with step 5 this proves the Hom bijection for every $X$, with no boundedness imposed on $B,G$, or $X$.

source.place: Tag 0149 (derived-lemma-representable-homological), clause (ii) before and after rotation; explicit injectivity chase

proof.text: Take $X=G$ in the surjectivity just proved to obtain $\beta:G\to B$ with $\alpha\beta=1_G$. Then $\alpha(\beta\alpha)=\alpha=\alpha1_B$. Injectivity for $X=B$ implies $\beta\alpha=1_B$. Hence $\beta$ is an inverse of $\alpha$, as required.

source.place: Conclusion: elementary two-sided inverse construction from the Hom bijections
